q_statement: In India, which one of the following Constitutional Amendments was widely believed to be enacted to overcome the judicial interpretations of the Fundamental Rights?
explanation:
Exp) Option a is the correct answer

Option a is correct: The First Amendment Act, 1951,
added the fourth clause to Article 15 that empowered the
government to make any law for the upliftment of sociaily
and educationally backward classes of citizens or for the
Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. It reads, “Nothing
in this article or in clause (2) of article 29 shall prevent the
State from making any special provision for the advancement
of any socially and educationally backward classes of citizens
or for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes.”. The
added clause elucidates that in case such special provisions
are introduced, they cannot be said to be breaching Article
15 and Article 29(2) of the Constitution.

The need to insert this clause was felt after the decision
of the Supreme Court in the State of Madras y. Srimathi
Champakam (1951). According to the facts of this case, the
Madras government issued an Order that provided reservation
on the grounds of religion, race, and caste. This Order was
contended to be in breach of Article 15(1) of the Indian
Constitution. The Court also gave a literal interpretation
to the constitutional provisions and held that reserving
seats in public institutions for backward classes violates
Articles 15(1) and 29(2). Vherefore, in order to nullify the
effect of similar judicial pronouncements, Article 15 was
amended.

Similarly, Article 19(1)(a) grants the right to free speech
and expression to Indian citizens. This right is considered
an essential feature of democracy. However, Article 19(2)
specifies the restrictions that can curtail this freedom. The
First Amendment to the Indian Constitution altered these
restrictions by widening their ambit. The second change, via
the Amendment Act of 1951, was made to Clause 6 of Article
19.

q_statement:
Consider the following Statements:

2. When a Constitution Amendment Bill is presented to the President of India, it is obligatory for the President of India to give his/her assent.

3. A Constitution Amendment Bill must ‘be passed by both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha by a special majority and there is no provision for joint sitting.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation:
Exp) Option b is the correct answer

Statement 1 is incorrect: Constitution Amendment Bill can
be introduced cither by a minister or by a private member
and does not require prior permission from the President.
Statement 2 is correct: The 24th Amendment of the Indian
Constitution amended Article 368 to provide expressly
that Parliament has the power to amend any provision of the
Constitution. The amendment further made it obligatory
for the President to give his assent when a Constitution
Amendment Bill was presented to him.

Statement 3 is correct: Article 368 of the Indian constitution
requires that the constitution of India can be amended
by both houses of parliament by a 2/3 majority(special
majority). In case of disagreement between both houses,
there is no provision to summon a joint session of
parliament. The reasoning behind this is so as to not let the

running government's majority in Lok Sabha undermine the

Rajya Sabha in a joint sitting.

q_statement:
What is the position of the right to property

in India?
a: Legal right available to citizens only
b: Legal right available to any person
c:
Fundamental Right available to citizens
only
d:
Neither Fundamental Right nor legal
right
explanation:
Exp) Option b is the correct answer,

The Right to Property is a legal right available to any

person. Article 300-A provides that no person shall be

deprived of his property save by authority of law.

Right to Property was a Fundamental Right in the original

constitution under Article 31, which provided that the

Constitution not only guarantees the right of private

ownership but'also the right to enjoy and dispose of property

free from restrictions other than reasonable restriction, It is
also mentioned that compensation would be paid to a person
whose property has been taken for public purposes.

The Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978

deleted the right to property from the Fundamental

Rights. The Amendment omitted Article 31 and Article 19

(1) (f) and inserted in their place Article 300-A.

q_statement:
With reference to the provisions contained
in Part IV of the Constitution of India,
which of the following statements is/are

correct?

2. They shall not be enforceable by any
court.

3. The principles laid down in this part are
to influence the making of laws by the
State.

Select the correct answer using the code given

below:
explanation:
Exp) Option d is the correct answer.

Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) are enshrined in

Part-IV (Article 36 to 51) of the Constitution.

Statement 1 is incorrect and statement 2 is correct. Article

37 of the Constitution states that the provisions contained in

this Part (IV) shall not be enforceable by any court.

Statement 3 is correct. The principles therein laid down are

nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country

and it shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles
in making laws. Hence, they impose a moral obligation on
the state authorities for their application.

Limitations of Part IV of the Indian Constitution:

1) No Legal Force: The DPSP are non-justiciable in nature
i.e. they are not legally enforceable by the courts for
their violation.

2) Constitutional Conflict: DPSP leads to constitutional
conflict between Centre and states, Centre and
President, Chief Minister and governor.

3) Conflict with Fundamental rights: They can be amended
to implement the fundamental rights.

4) Constitutional validity: A law cannot be struck down by
courts for violating DPSP.

Constitution would be the freedom of choice in marriage”.
This was reiterated by Supreme court in 2017, The choice of
a partner whether within or outside marriage lies within the
exclusive domain of cach individual. Intimacies of marriage
lie within a core zone of privacy, which is inviolable. The
absolute right of an individual to choose a life partner is not
in the least affected by matters of faith, The Constitution
guarantces to each individual the right freely to practise,
profess and propagate religion.

being entered in the clectoral roll of any constituency shall
be entitled to vote in that constituency”.

eighteen years of age is entitled to get enrolled into electoral
roll and is entitled to vote in the constituency in which his
name is entered in the electoral roll irrespective of caste,
creed, religion or gender unless he is disqualified under
the Constitution or any other law on the ground of non-
residence, unsoundness of mind, crime or corrupt or illegal
practice.

and forced labour

3. Protection of the interests of minorities

factories and mines

explanation:
Exp) Option cis the correct answer.

The Right against Exploitation under Articles 23 and 24

of the Indian Constitution guarantees the dignity of the

individual. Under these -

labour) and other similar forms of forced labour. Any

contravention of this provision shall be an offence punishable

in accordance with law. This right is available to both citizens

1. legislative function.
2. executive function.

explanation:
Exp) Option d is the correct answer.

As Directive Principles of State Policy are not justiciable, they

do not constitute limitations upon legislative and executive

function of the state. The phrase ‘Directive Principles of

State Policy’ denotes the ideals that the State should keep

in mind while formulating policies and enacting laws. These

are the constitutional instructions or recommendations to

the State in legislative, executive and administrative matters.

According to Article 36, the term ‘State’ in Part IV has the

same meaning as in Part III dealing with Fundamental Rights.

Therefore, it includes the legislative and executive organs of

the central and state governments, all local authorities and

all other public authorities in the country.

q_statement:
In the context of India, which one of
the following is the correct relationship
between Rights and Duties?
b:
Rights are personal and _ hence
independent of society and Duties.
c:
Rights, not Duties, are important for the
advancement of the personality of the
citizen.
d:
Duties, not Rights, are important for the
stability of the State.
explanation:
Exp) Option a is the correct answer.

With reference to the Constitution of India, it can be said

that the Rights are correlative with Duties. Every right

has a corresponding duty. Therefore, there can be no duty

unless there is someone to whom it is due. There can be

no right without a corresponding duty or a duty without a

corresponding right. Likewise, every right is right against

some person or persons upon whom a correlative duty is
imposed. Every right or duty involves a legal obligation by
which two or more persons are bound together.

Under Indian Constitution, Part HII deals with the

Fundamental Rights which are certain basic human rights

to its people. Our Constitution as originally enacted did not

expressly lay down any Fundamental Duties to be performed

by citizens. It was only in 1976 that a specific Chapter IV-A

was incorporated in the Constitution by a constitutional

amendment and Article 51-A was enacted. The idea
behind the incorporation of the Fundamental Duties was
to emphasize the obligation of the citizen in exchange of

Fundamental Rights enjoyed by them.

q_statement:
The basic structure theory of the

Constitution of India Implies that-
a:
Certain features of the Constitution
are so essential to it that they cannot be
abrogated.
b:
Fundamental rights cannot be abridged
or taken away.
c:
The Constitution cannot be amended
except in accordance with the procedure
laid down in Article 368.
d:
The Preamble of the Constitution
cannot be amended for it is not a part
of the Constitution and at the same time
represents its real spirit.
explanation:
Exp) Option a is the correct answer.
The basic structure doctrine is a judicial principle
established by the Supreme Court of India. According to
this doctrine, certain features or elements of the Indian
Constitution are considered so fundamental and essential
that they form the basic structure of the Constitution.
These features cannot be abrogated or altered even through
the process of Constitutional amendment under Article 368.
The Supreme Court has held that while Parliament
has the power to amend the Constitution, it cannot use
this power to destroy or alter the basic structure of the
Constitution. The Court has not provided an exhaustive
list of elements that constitute the basic structure, but some
of the features considered as part of the basic structure
include the supremacy of the Constitution, the rule of law,
the independence of the judiciary, the secular nature of the
statc, federalism, and the basic rights guaranteed to citizens.
Important Tipss

The basic structure doctrine has been invoked by |

the Supreme Court in several cases to strike down

constitutional amendments that were found to be violative |
of the basic structure. Some examples are: |

* Indira Nehru Gandhi v Raj Narain (1975), where clause |
(4) of article 329A, which immunized the election of |
Prime Minister from judicial scrutiny, was struck down |
as it violated democracy and rule of law. :

e Minerva Mills v Union of India (1980), where clauses |
(4) and (5) of article 368, which gave unlimited |
amending power to parliament and excluded judicial !
review, were struck down as they destroyed harraony |
between fundamental rights and directive principles. |

¢ S.R. Bommai v Union of India (1994), where arbitrary
use of article 356, which empowers President to impose |
President’s rule in states, was held to be violative of |
federalism and democracy. i

« LR. Coelho v State of Tamil Nadu (2007), where it was |
held that laws placed in Ninth Schedule after April 24, ;
1973 (the date of Kesavananda Bharati judgement) are |
open to judicial review if they violate basic structure.

q_statement:
Given below are two statements, one is
labelled as Assertion (A) and the other as
Reason (R):

Assertion (A): The State can treat unequal

differently with the objective of creating a

level playing field in the social, economic and

political spheres.

Reason (R): Among equals the law should be

equal and equally administered.

In the context of the above statements select

the correct answer
c:
Both (A) and (R) are correct, but (R) is
not the correct explanation of (A).
d:
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the
correct explanation of (A).
explanation:
Exp) Option d is the correct answer.
Assertion (A) is correct: State can treat unequal differently
with the objective of creating a level playing field in the
social, economic and political spheres. This is based on the
principle of equal protection of laws, which means that the
law gives equal opportunities to all people who are in similar
circumstances or situations. This principle allows the State
to make reasonable classifications among people and provide
special provisions or reservations for the advancement
of any backward class of citizens, which is not adequately
represented in the services under the State. This is done
to ensure substantive equality and not merely formal
equality.
Reason (R) is correct statement: Among equals the law
should be equal and equally administered. This is based on
the principle of equality before law, which means that no one
is above the rule of law. This principle implies that all people
are subject to the same laws and the same judicial system,
regardless of their status or power.

Reason (R) is also the correct explanation of Assertion (A)

because it implies that the State can treat unequal differently

only with the objective of creating equality among them.

The State cannot discriminate among equals or favour any

group without a reasonable basis. The special provisions for

the backward classes and the scheduled castes and tribes
are based on the reasonable classification of these groups
as being under-represented and deserving of preferential
treatment to achieve substantive equality.
Important Tipss
« Equality before law is a negative concept that restricts
the State from engaging in any arbitrary discrimination
between individuals.
« Equal protection of laws is a positive concept that
puts a positive obligation on the State to prevent the
violation of rights.

e Equality before law does not mean that all laws must be
general in character and universal in application. Equal
protection of laws does not mean that all laws must be
alike for all people without any distinction.

« Equality before law deals with equal subjection of all
persons to the ordinary law of the land administered
by ordinary law courts. Equal protection of laws deals
with similar application of the same laws to all persons
who are similarly situated

of his life or personal liberty except according to the
procedure established by law”.

amendment made in contravention of this principle would
be void.

of Parliament.

* However, the Golaknath case was itself overruled by

limits the Parliament’s amending power to preserve the
essential features of the Constitution.

to equal pay for equal work from the word ‘socialist’ used
in the Preamble to the Constitution as well as from Article

Equal pay for equal work is not a constitutional right
or a fundamental right. It can be described through the
interpretations of Article 14, 15 and 16 which guarantee
fundamental rights of equality before law, protection against
any kind of discrimination and equal opportunities in the
matters of public employment.

The word ‘socialist? used in the Preamble to the Constitution
also enabled the Supreme Court of India to deduce a
fundamental right to equal pay for equal work. The Preamble
declares India to bea sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic
republic. The term ‘socialist’ implies social and economic
justice for all citizens. It also implies that the State shall
strive to reduce inequalities in income, status, facilities and
opportunities among individuals and groups

the courts, subject to certain restrictions. They protect the
citizens from arbitrary or discriminatory state action that
violatcs or abridges their rights.

Articles 12 to 35 of Part III of the Constitution of India.
There are six Fundamental Rights, namely, Right to Equality,
Right to Freedom, right against Exploitation, Right to

Right to Constitutional Remedies.

justice, which is more of a goal of the Directive Principles

heavily inspired by the Bill of Rights in the U.S.A., which

is the first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution that
guarantee civil liberties to the people. The Fundamental

Rights in India have their origins in many sources, including

England’s Bill of Rights, the United States Bill of Rights and

France’s Declaration of the Rights of Man.

Constitution of India, These are:

right to shelter is a part of the right to life and personal
liberty under Article 21 of the Constitution. It means
that every citizen has the right to adequate housing
that ensures human dignity, privacy, and security. The
Supreme Court has also held that the State has a duty to
provide shelter to the poor, homeless, and marginalized
sections of society.

of movement under Article 19 (1) (d) of the Constitution.

restriction or interference by the State. The Supreme
Court has also held that the State can impose reasonable
restrictions on this right in the interests of sovereignty,

integrity, and security of India, friendly relations with
foreign states, public order, or morality under Article 19
(5) of the Constitution.

» Right to Equal Pay for Equal Work: ‘The Supreme Court
has held that the right to equal pay for equal work is
a part of the right to equality under Article 14 and 16
of the Constitution. It means that every citizen has the
right to receive equal remuneration for work of equal
value without any discrimination on the grounds of
sex, caste, religion, etc . The Supreme Court has also
held that this right is a constitutional goal that is to be
attained by the State in accordance with Article 39 (d) of

policy.

q_statement:
Which one of the following writs is regarded

as the greatest safeguard for the liberty of a

person?
explanation:
Exp) Option b is the correct answer.

The writ of Habeas Corpus is regarded as the greatest
safeguard for the liberty of a person. Habeas Corpus is a

Latin term that means “to have the body.” It is a legal action
through which a person can challenge the lawfulness of
their detention or imprisonment. The writ is used to seek
the release of a person who is unlawfully detained or held
against their will.

The purpose of the writ of Habeas Corpus is to protect
individual liberty and ensure that a person is not
unlawfully deprived of their freedom. It is considered a
fundamental safeguard against arbitrary or illegal detention,
providing a mechanism for individuals to challenge the
lawfulness of their detention before a court of law.

Important Tipss

« Mandamus: This writ means ‘we command? It is used to
order a public official, a public body, a corporation, an
inferior court, a tribunal or a government to perform
a dutythat they are obliged to perform but have failed
orferused to do so.

¢ Prohibition: This writ means ‘to forbid’ It is used to
stop an inferior court, a tribunal or an authority from
exceeding its jurisdiction or acting contrary to the rules
of natural justice. It prevents them from continuing a
proceeding that is ultra vires or invalid.

+ Certiorari: This writ means ‘to be certified’ It is used
to transfer a case pending before an inferior court, a
tribunal or an authority to a higher court for review.
It can also be used to quash or nullify an order already
passed by an inferior court, a tribunal or an authority
that is ultra vires, unconstitutional, illegal, erroneous
or without jurisdiction.

e Quo Warranto: This writ means ‘by what authority’. It
is used to challenge the legality of a person’s claim to
hold a public office. It prevents usurpation of public
office by an ineligible or unqualified person. It can also
be used to oust such person from the office if he or she
is already holding it

explanation:

The rule of law is a political and legal principle that means

all people and institutions are subject to and accountable

to law that is fairly applied and enforced. It also implies

that no one is above the law, that the government is not

arbitrary, and that the laws are consistent and impartial.

In India, the rule of law is enshrined in the Constitution,

which prescribes the ideas of justice, liberty and equality for

all citizens. The Constitution also provides for separation of

principles of state policy to ensure that the rule of law is

upheld in the country.

judiciary for all. This option reflects the idea that everyone

regardless of their status or power.

q_statement:
Select the correct chronological order of
the following judgements dealing with
Fundamental Rights:

(A) Golaknath v/s State of Punjab
(B) Keshvananda Bharati v/s State of Kerala
(C) Minerva Mills v/s Union of India
(D) A.K Gopalan v/s State of Madras
Select the correct answer:
explanation:
Exp) Option c is the correct answer.

The correct chronological order of the judgements dealing

with Fundamental Rights is:

(D)A.K Gopalan v/s State of Madras (1956) - This case
dealt with the validity of preventive detention and the
scope of Article 21 of the Constitution. The Supreme
Court held that the Fundamental Rights are not absolute
and can be restricted by law. It also held that each
Fundamental Right is separate and distinct, and there is
no inter-relationship between them.

(A)Golaknath v/s State of Punjab (1967) - This case
dealt with the power of Parliament to amend the
Fundamental Rights. The Supreme Court overruled
its previous decisions and held that Parliament cannot
amend the Fundamental Rights, as they are sacrosanct
and transcendental. It also held that Article 368 only lays
down the procedure for amendment, and any amendment
is a law under Article 13, which cannot abridge or take
away the Fundamental Rights.

(B) Keshvananda Bharati v/s State of Kerala (1973) - This
case dealt with the validity of the 24th, 25th and 29th
Amendment Acts, which curtailed the Fundamental
Rights relating to property and introduced the doctrine
of basic structure. The Supreme Court overruled
the Golaknath case and upheld the validity of these
amendments. It held that Parliament has the power

to amend any part of the Constitution, including the
Fundamental Rights, but it cannot alter or destroy the
basic structure or essential features of the Constitution.

(C) Minerva Mills v/s Union of India (1980) - This case
dealt with the validity of the 42nd Amendment Act,
which inserted two clauses in Article 368, giving power
to Parliament to amend any part of the Constitution,
including the basic structure, and making such
amendments immune from judicial review. The Supreme
Court struck down these clauses as unconstitutional and
violative of the basic structure. It reaffirmed the doctrine
of basic structure and held that there is a harmony
and balance between the Fundamental Rights and the
Directive Principles, which constitute the core of the
basic structure.

Important Tipss

Minerva Mill Case:

Rights and Directive Principles.

and secular character of the polity, the separation of

q_statement:
The rights are called Fundamental Rights
because
i. It is written in the Constitution.
ii. It is democratic.

ii, iii, v

Exp) Option c is the correct answer.

The rights are called Fundamental Rights because:

are enshrined in Part III of the Constitution of India from
Article 12 to 35 and are guaranteed to all citizens.

iv. It is essential for personality development. The

Fundamental Rights are defined as basic human freedoms

where every Indian citizen has the right to enjoy for a proper

and harmonious development of personality and life.

Rights are enforceable by the courts, subject to certain

restrictions, and any law made by the Parliament that

violates or abridges the Fundamental Rights can be declared

« Although the Fundamental Rights are essential for a
democratic system, they are not exclusively democratic
in nature. There are other forms of government that may
also grant some civil liberties to their citizens, such as
constitutional monarchy or republicanism.

« The Fundamental Rights are not necessarily related to

Principles of State Policy (Part IV of the Constitution).

individual rights and liberties that protect the citizens
from arbitrary state action or discrimination.

q_statement:
What is correct about external emergency
as per Article 352?
i. It is proclaimed by the President.
ii. It should be approved by Parliament within
two months.
iii. It should be approved by Parliament
within one month.
iv. It should be approved by Parliament by a
simple majority.

2/3 majority.

Parliament.

Parliament.
viii. It can be approved in a joint session of
Parliament.

i, iv, vii, viii
(e) None of the above
explanation:
Exp) Option cis the correct answer

When a national emergency is declared on the ground of ‘war’

or ‘external aggression’ it is known as ‘External Emergency’.

On the other hand, when it is declared on the ground of

‘armed rebellion’ it is known as ‘Internal Emergency’. As per

Article 352, the President can declare a national emergency

when the security of India is threatened by war/external

aggression/armed rebellion. The proclamation of Emergency
must be approved by both the Houses of Parliament within
one month. If approved by both the Houses of Parliament, the
emergency continues for six months. For the proclamation
of emergency or its continuance, the resolution must be
passed by either House of Parliament by a special majority.

A revocation of emergency does not require parliamentary

approval. It can be revoked by the President at any time by a

subsequent proclamation. The emergency must be revoked

if the Lok Sabha passes a resolution by a simple majority
disapproving of its continuation.

q_statement:
By which of the following grounds, a
citizen’s freedom of expression may not be
subjected to restriction?
d:
Unbecoming criticism
(e) All of the above
explanation:
Exp) Option d is the correct answer.

Freedom of expression is a fundamental! right guaranteed by
Article 19 (1) (a) of the Constitution of India. It includes
the right to express one’s views and opinions through any
mode of communication, such as words, signs, symbols,
gestures, pictures, etc. It also includes the right to receive
and impart information from any source and disseminate it
to others.
However, freedom of expression is not absolute or unlimited.
It is subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by the State
under Article 19 (2) of the Constitution. These restrictions
can be imposed in the interests of the sovereignty and
integrity of India, the security of the State, friendly
relations with foreign States, public order, decency or
morality, contempt of court, defamation or incitement to
an offence.
Unbecoming criticism is not one of the grounds on which
freedom of expression can be restricted. Unbecoming
criticism means criticism that is inappropriate, improper, or
disrespectful. However, such criticism may not necessarily
violate any of the grounds mentioned in Article 19 (2) of the
Constitution.
